title: Be a Ford, Then a Sloan
author: Sahil Bloom
summary: Bloom sets Henry Ford against Alfred Sloan to argue that the operating style which creates a thing is rarely the one that sustains it. Ford's atomic insight was to treat the factory as the product, an obsession with footsteps and minutes that drove the Model T from 850 dollars to 260 and gave Ford sixty percent of the American market. The same rigidity then blinded him, and Bloom recounts Ford physically tearing apart a refined prototype his team had built and rebuking his son Edsel for noticing that buyers now wanted status and variety. Sloan's insight at General Motors was to treat the company itself as the product, designing divisions, decentralised decisions, data tracking and financial control so the organisation could shift as the market did. Bloom resists the easy moral of Ford bad, Sloan good, pointing out that Sloan's structure would have strangled a zero to one venture and Ford's would always have failed later. The practical turn asks readers to diagnose which mode they are in and to run a regular cadence of course correction questions, including which delayed decision is being avoided out of fear of disappointing someone.
points: The contrast is framed as two atomic insights, the factory as the product against the company as the product.
Bloom uses the destroyed prototype and the rebuke of Edsel to show a founder's greatest strength hardening into his constraint.
He explicitly rejects the Ford bad Sloan good reading, arguing Sloan's design would not have survived the zero to one phase.
The pattern is extended to health, relationships and money, where routines that fit one decade stop fitting the next.
The course correction questions force a single-variable choice and surface decisions delayed out of fear of letting someone down.
quotes: While others obsessed over the car, he obsessed over the optimization of the factory. Every single worker's footstep. Every single minute of production time. Every single constraint. These became his sole focus.

Henry Ford's son, Edsel, whom he had appointed President of the company, began noticing that consumer preferences were changing. With the abundance of simple, black Model Ts on the road, some consumers seemed to be looking for something different.
The maniacal attention to detail and systematized rigor that had served him had now come to own him.

Rather than a rigid structure with him as the sole decision maker, Sloan designed an organization with clear divisions of labor, decentralized decision making, proper data tracking, and strategic financial control.

Ford's approach worked, until it didn't. Ruthless attention to detail. Centralized decision making. Narrow, refined focus. All of these attributes and organizational principles enabled the extraordinary innovation that makes Henry Ford a household name today.
But the skillset, systems, and structure that can get you to your first million aren't the same as the ones that can get you from one to ten million, or again from ten to one hundred million.

What decision have I been delaying for fear of letting someone down? I find that one of the most common walls for leaders is the fear of disappointing others. But those hard conversations you delay just make for harder conversations later.
